summary: Defines a simple extension for RTP sessions where redundant copies of media are sent before the primary data, a forward-shifted redundancy. This can conceal the loss of many consecutive frames, even seconds of media.

eli5.summary: If you send the same sentence early as well as on time, a short gap in the line will not make you miss it. This lets audio and video repeat information ahead of time to survive longer outages.

questions: what is the fwdred media type
what does forwardshift mean in sdp
how does rtp conceal long packet loss
subtitle: Send the backup copy of media before the main copy, so a long radio blackout does not interrupt playback.

tldr.problem: RFC 2198 sends redundant media after the primary data, which cannot cover the loss of many consecutive frames, such as a mobile receiver sitting in a radio shadow for seconds or tens of seconds.
tldr.mechanism: A new media type, fwdred, carries a forwardshift parameter that tells the receiver how far ahead of the primary data the redundant blocks are sent, so the receiver can buffer them and play from them during an outage.
tldr.outcome: A receiver that holds the next forwardshift worth of redundant frames can ride out any shadow no longer than that shift. This RFC updates RFC 2198 and RFC 4102.

facts.label: Example shift
facts.value: 155 frames, 3.1 seconds at 20 ms per frame

today: RFC 6354 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2198 and RFC 4102. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Redundancy Must Move Forward
sections.content:
This document is a small enhancement to RFC 2198 for RTP sessions. It supports forward-shifted redundant encodings, meaning the redundant data is sent before the matching primary data.

The motivating case is a mobile receiver whose radio signal is blocked by tall buildings, mountains or tunnels. The RFC calls this a shadow: no new data arrives while the receiver is in it, sometimes for seconds or even tens of seconds. Traditional backward-shifted redundancy, where the copy follows the primary data, does not help with such long runs of lost frames.

For live media there is a cost. The sender must generate the forward-shifted stream, so it needs to insert a delay at the source equal to or greater than the amount of forward-shifting. Pre-recorded media can use the scheme without that delay.
sections.eli5: Sending a backup after the real thing does not help if the line is dead for a long time. Sending the backup first means you already have it when the line drops.

sections.title: Allowing Forward-Shifted Redundant Data
sections.content:
In RFC 2198 the timestamp offset in the additional header of a redundant block is a 14-bit unsigned value, subtracted from the RTP header timestamp. An unsigned offset can only point backward in time, so it effectively prevents forward-shifted blocks.

This RFC introduces the media type fwdred with a parameter forwardshift. It signals both the capability and willingness to use forward-shifted redundancy and the base value of the shift, an integer of 0 or more in RTP timestamp units. The timestamp of a redundant block is then:

timestamp of redundant block = timestamp in RTP header - timestamp offset in additional header + forward-shift base value

In a forward-shifted session the offset in the additional header is generally set to 0. The sender MUST NOT change the contents of a packet that appears in a forward-shifted stream when it is later time to send it in the main stream.
sections.eli5: The old scheme could only say 'this backup is for something a moment ago'. The new one adds a fixed number saying 'this backup is for something that far in the future'.

sections.title: The fwdred Media Type
sections.content:
The registration is based on the red media type from RFC 2198 and RFC 4102, plus the forwardshift parameter. The type names are audio and text, and the subtype is fwdred.

  • rate and pt are required and defined as in RFC 4102.
  • forwardshift is required and holds an unsigned integer in RTP timestamp units. A value above 0 means the sender will forward-shift its redundant data by that base value. A value of 0 means no forward-shifting, so the sender behaves as in RFC 2198.
  • ptime and maxptime are optional.

The type is framed binary data and is defined only for transfer over RTP.
sections.eli5: The new label has one extra setting, 'how far ahead'. Setting it to zero means 'do it the old way'.

sections.title: Describing It in SDP
sections.content:
In the Session Description Protocol the media type audio goes in the m= line, the subtype fwdred goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name, and forwardshift=value is copied into the a=fmtp attribute.

The RFC gives an example indicating a forward shift of 5.1 seconds, with forwardshift=40800 and a clock rate of 8000. A second example with forwardshift=0 is equivalent to RFC 2198.

In offer/answer use, the parameter is declarative, and all reasonable values are expected to be supported.
sections.eli5: The call setup message simply lists the 'how far ahead' number so both sides agree before the music starts.

sections.title: Anti-Shadow Receiver Behavior
sections.content:
The informational appendix describes anti-shadow loss concealment. The sender adds a forward-shifted redundant stream, the AS stream, next to the primary stream. The amount of shift should stay constant for the session and sets the longest shadow that can be fully concealed.

The receiver has two modes. In normal mode it plays the primary data and stores the AS data in an anti-shadow buffer, purging any frame older than the last primary frame played. The buffer is always full, holding the next forwardshift worth of redundant frames. In AS mode, entered when new data stops arriving, it keeps playing from the buffer. When data returns it switches back at once and refills the buffer.

If the shadow lasts longer than the forward shift, the buffer runs out and service is interrupted.

In the worked example the shift is 155 frames, which is 3.1 seconds at 20 ms per frame. A receiver entering a shadow at t=3120 can keep playing until t=6240.
sections.eli5: While the line is good, you copy tomorrow's notes into a notebook. When the line dies you read from the notebook, and it only runs out if the line stays dead longer than the notes cover.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 2198, RFC 4856 and RFC 3550 apply. In addition, to prevent denial-of-service attacks, a receiver SHOULD be prepared to ignore a forwardshift declaration if it considers the offset excessive. In that case it SHOULD also ignore the redundant stream in the resulting RTP session.
sections.eli5: If someone claims the backup is a ridiculous distance ahead, the receiver can say no thanks and ignore the backup.

data.title: Forward shift of 5.1 seconds
data.code:
m=audio 12345 RTP/AVP 121 0 5
a=rtpmap:121 fwdred/8000/1
a=fmtp:121 0/5 forwardshift=40800
